terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where try.js posts a good quote, broken JSON, bad fields and an oversized body to your API.

tasks.title: Collect the body
tasks.description:
Implement `readBody(req, limit = 10000)` in `src/body.js`.

It resolves to the whole request body as a UTF-8 string:

- an empty body resolves to `''`
- a body of exactly `limit` bytes is fine
- a body larger than `limit` **bytes** rejects with `new HttpError(413, 'payload_too_large', message)`

The check starts a small server around your `readBody` and posts real bodies to it, including one where the number of characters and the number of bytes differ.
nextSteps: Loop over the request with `for await` and look at what each chunk is.
Keep a running total of bytes and stop as soon as it goes over the limit.
Join the chunks and turn them into a string at the end.
Press Check, then run `node try.js` once `readJson` is done too.
hints: A request is a stream. It arrives in pieces, and you only have the body once the stream ends.
Each chunk is a Buffer, and a Buffer's `length` is already in bytes. Count those, not characters.
Push each chunk into an array and add its length to a total. Throw the HttpError when the total passes `limit`, and return `Buffer.concat(chunks).toString('utf8')` at the end.

tasks.title: Parse it as JSON
tasks.description:
Implement `readJson(req, limit = 10000)` in `src/body.js`.

- read the body with `readBody(req, limit)`, so large bodies still get 413
- resolve to the parsed value
- an empty body, or text that is not valid JSON, rejects with `new HttpError(400, 'invalid_json', message)`

A `SyntaxError` escaping from here would become a 500, which tells the client the server broke when it was the request that was wrong. The check calls `readJson` directly and also posts broken JSON to `POST /quotes`.
nextSteps: Parse the text and turn a parse failure into the right HttpError.
Run `node try.js` and look at the second request.
hints: Ask yourself who made the mistake when parsing fails. The status code should say so.
`JSON.parse('')` throws too, but its message is confusing. A clear message for an empty body helps the client.
Wrap only `JSON.parse(text)` in try and catch, and throw `new HttpError(400, 'invalid_json', ...)` from the catch.

tasks.title: Check the fields
tasks.description:
Implement `validateQuote(input)` in `src/quote.js`. It runs on the parsed body of `POST /quotes` and returns `{ type, hours }`, with no other fields.

Rules:

- `input` must be a plain object, not `null` and not an array
- `type` must be one of the keys of `RATES` (`single`, `double`, `paddleboard`)
- `hours` must be a whole number from 1 to 8, sent as a number

When anything is wrong, throw `new HttpError(400, 'validation_failed', message, details)`. `details` is an array with one `{ field, message }` entry per problem, and it lists **every** problem at once, so `{}` gives entries for both `type` and `hours`.

The check calls `validateQuote` with many inputs, including a type name that every object has.
nextSteps: Reject anything that is not a plain object first.
Collect problems in an array instead of throwing on the first one.
Throw once at the end if the array is not empty, otherwise return the two fields.
Run `node try.js` and read the details of the third request.
hints: JSON gives you whatever the client sent. Check the type of each value, not just whether it is there.
`typeof null` is `'object'` and so is `typeof []`. You need more than one test for a plain object.
`'toString' in RATES` is true and `RATES.toString` exists. `Object.hasOwn(RATES, type)` only sees the keys you wrote. For hours, `Number.isInteger` rejects strings and fractions in one go.
